strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with empirical validation: clearly articulates limitations of existing LoRA-based CL methods and validates through relative projection energy analysis (Figure 3)

Theoretically grounded approach: projection energy provides intuitive insight into LoRA's learning capacity (Theorem 3.1) and enables principled subspace decomposition with closed-form solutions (Theorems 3.2-3.3)
Principled subspace design: decomposition objectives (maximizing E_old+E_new for general subspace, E_new/E_old for isolated) avoid arbitrary constraints of prior orthogonal-based methods
Comprehensive experimental validation: consistent improvements across 5 datasets with multiple task configurations, thorough ablations (Table 3), and informative visualizations (Figures 5-6)
Elegant closed-form recalibration (Eq. 12-13) that avoids local linearity approximations and gradient-based estimates, comparing favorably to existing merging strategies
Computational efficiency: no additional inference parameters/overhead; storage overhead scales with model size not number of tasks
Clear presentation with effective figures communicating the core ideas, particularly Figures 1, 2, and 3
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: dual-branch LoRA (BiLoRA, PLAN), projection energy (straightforward concept), and recalibration are well-known ideas—core contribution is their combination rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient motivation for GAO: Eq. 11 introduced abruptly with unclear connection to projection energy framework; why gradient alignment is needed after fixing down-projections is not well justified; limited ablation showing 0.34%-1.89% improvement

Hyperparameter sensitivity concerns: multiple hyperparameters (w_G=0.5, λ=3.0, ρ_max=0.7/0.3) with minimal sensitivity analysis; Table 5 suggests some sensitivity to λ; selection criteria not explained
Missing appendix references: page 4 contains two 'Appx. ??' placeholders indicating incomplete submission preparation

Incomplete analysis of theoretical assumptions: Theorem 3.2 assumes full-rank S_{1:t-1} based on 'huge sample size' justification, but no numerical stability discussion, conditioning analysis, or treatment of early-task scenarios with limited data

Limited task correlation analysis: motivates approach for correlated tasks but provides minimal analysis; no experiments varying task correlation levels; Figure 6 shows projections but not explicit correlation characterization
Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: O(LD²) storage grows with model size; 27MB for ViT-B/16 may be problematic for larger models or very long task streams; no scaling behavior analysis
Statistical rigor gaps: no significance testing despite reporting standard deviations; some improvements within error margins; unclear if all differences are statistically significant

Incomplete empirical analysis: Table 4 compares isolation methods only for LoRAI without LoRAG; semantic interpretation of what U_G and U_I capture is limited; missing ablations on weighting schemes for E_old+E_new
Limited failure case analysis: no experiments on highly imbalanced tasks, tasks with different complexities, or dissimilar task streams; unclear when method would underperform
LoDA+CA with feature replay shows much larger gains than LoDA alone, suggesting method may be particularly suited to replay strategy; unclear if advantage generalizes to other replay methods
Notation inconsistencies (S^t vs S_t) and presentation issues; Figure 2 is dense; missing discussion positioning work relative to other projection-based/energy-based methods

strengths: Novel projection energy perspective providing principled foundation for LoRA subspace decomposition in continual learning
Addresses demonstrated limitation of null-space based methods (Fig. 3) with well-motivated relative energy objective
Exact closed-form solutions for subspace computation (Theorems 3.2, 3.3) more principled than gradient-based approximations in prior work
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 5 datasets, multiple configurations, thorough ablations, extensive analysis (projection energy, loss landscapes, hyperparameters)
Generalization demonstrated on CLIP and self-supervised backbones with consistent improvements
Clear presentation with effective motivation, good figures, and detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameter ablations
weaknesses: Practical improvements modest (1-2% typically), with diminishing gains on easier datasets (CIFAR100, CUB) raising questions about practical significance

Key design choices lack sufficient theoretical justification: relative energy objective intuitively motivated but lacks formal guarantee of minimizing interference; GAO algorithm relies on strong gradient cone assumptions only validated to first order
Assumption that S_{1:t-1} is full rank (Theorem 3.2) not addressed for practical near-singular cases; numerical robustness unclear
First-order approximations (Theorems 3.1, B.4.5) not empirically validated; gap between theory and practice with dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning (ρ_max varies: 0.7 vs 0.3)
Limited scope: method specific to LoRA in vision CL; cannot apply to other PEFT paradigms or non-vision tasks
Statistical significance of 1-2% improvements not formally tested; contribution of orthogonal CA component not cleanly separated from main method

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Compelling empirical evidence (Fig. 3) that null-space-based isolation fails under correlated task distributions, addressing real limitations in prior LoRA-based CL methods
Solid theoretical foundation: Theorem 3.1 elegantly connects LoRA capacity to feature projection energy with exact closed-form solutions (Theorems 3.2-3.3) rather than approximations

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive benchmarks across 5 datasets with multiple settings (5S/10S/20S), 20+ baselines, multiple backbones (ViT, CLIP, DINO, iBOT), and model sizes, with consistent improvements of 0.8-1.7% ALast without replay
Practical efficiency: Zero extra parameters at inference, task-count-independent storage (27MB for ViT-B/16), with transparent overhead analysis and no need for storing past-task models

Thorough analysis: Effective ablation studies clearly demonstrating each component's contribution, loss landscape visualizations validating the approach, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis with multiple design choices explored
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Individual components are incremental (projection energy is intuitive but not fundamentally new; GAO adapts existing gradient-alignment ideas; closed-form recalibration applies standard optimization), with contribution primarily in their integration rather than novel concepts

Theory-practice gaps: Theorem 3.1 derived for single gradient step while practice uses many iterations; Theorem B.4 relies on strong assumptions (local linearity, cone decomposition) with limited empirical validation; no analysis of behavior under feature distribution shift

Unjustified design choices: No ablation for why E_old + E_new (not alternatives) defines general subspace; relative energy ratio (E_new/E_old) is heuristic without justification; hyperparameter sensitivity (w_G, λ, ρ_max) requires dataset-specific tuning per Fig. 8
Modest improvements on easier benchmarks: CIFAR100 (0.27% improvement with overlapping error bars), CUB (0.04%, essentially tied), suggesting benefits may be dataset-dependent rather than universal

Limited failure mode analysis: No discussion of failure scenarios, task ordering sensitivity, or extreme task distributions; only 3 random seeds (modern standard is 5-10); statistical significance tests not reported despite claiming superiority; recalibration assumptions not empirically validated
